title: SelectiveNet: A Deep Neural Network with an Integrated Reject Option
abstract: Introduces an end-to-end neural architecture that jointly optimizes prediction and rejection rather than thresholding a separately trained classifier. Experiments evaluate the resulting risk-coverage tradeoff on classification and regression tasks.

admission.reason: The reject-option and risk-coverage capability is relevant in principle, but the abstract concerns generic classification and regression and does not address NLP, free-form generation, temporal change or continuing distribution shift. The current corpus already contains selective-risk components; this paper does not materially close the remaining non-stationary communication gap.

title: Towards Improving Selective Prediction Ability of NLP Systems
abstract: Studies selective prediction in NLP under both in-domain and out-of-domain conditions. It trains a calibrator using model confidence and instance difficulty to predict correctness and evaluates whether abstention can improve reliability under distribution shift.

admission.reason: The paper studies NLP selective prediction and out-of-domain reliability, but the remaining gap is continuing temporal or non-stationary change in free-form communication. The project status explicitly says cross-domain calibration studies are already present, so a static in-domain versus out-of-domain study does not materially strengthen the unresolved capability.

title: SelfCheckGPT: Zero-Resource Black-Box Hallucination Detection for Generative Large Language Models
abstract: Proposes a sampling-based method for detecting factual hallucinations without an external evidence database or access to model probabilities. It evaluates sentence-level factuality and passage-level ranking against human annotations, providing a transfer baseline for uncertainty-based factuality screening.

admission.reason: The paper detects hallucination through sampling consistency without external source evidence. That can screen model uncertainty, but it does not determine whether a claim is supported by the actual evidence, whether attribution is correct, whether evidence is complete, or whether current-state information was omitted. Its topic vocabulary overlaps F1, but the required evidence-grounded capability does not.

title: Hierarchical Group-Conditional Conformal Risk Control for Selective Prediction in Language Models
abstract: Extends conformal risk control for selective prediction in language models to heterogeneous groups structured by domain, topic difficulty, and linguistic style. It addresses the limitation that a marginal risk guarantee can conceal subgroup-specific overexposure to errors.

admission.reason: Group-conditional selective risk in language models is relevant to heterogeneous error exposure, but the abstract does not address temporal evolution or continual adaptation. For this round it does not materially close gap-8, and subgroup conditioning is secondary to the unresolved non-stationary-stream requirement.

title: Conformal PID Control for Time Series Prediction
abstract: Combines conformal prediction with control-theoretic feedback to adapt uncertainty sets in the presence of seasonality, trends, systematic error, and general distribution shifts. Its online adaptation machinery is a transfer candidate for temporally changing calibration problems.

admission.reason: The online adaptation mechanism is relevant transfer theory, but it is demonstrated for time-series prediction and is less directly aligned than the admitted online conformal papers that explicitly handle arbitrary or detected distribution drift. With scarce reading slots, this would add another transfer mechanism without materially strengthening the free-form communication question.

title: Selective Classification for Deep Neural Networks
abstract: Develops selective classification for deep neural networks, allowing a user to specify a desired risk level while the system rejects enough predictions to meet that risk with high probability. Evaluation explicitly couples risk and coverage, making it a foundational transfer result for calibrated abstention.

admission.reason: This is foundational selective-classification work, but the abstract is generic deep-network classification and does not address NLP, long-form generation or non-stationary streams. More directly relevant selective-generation and online-calibration candidates are available, so this paper would consume a slot without materially strengthening the unresolved gaps.

title: Conformal Prediction for Natural Language Processing: A Survey
abstract: Surveys conformal prediction methods and applications across NLP, including generation and hallucination-risk control. It emphasizes that ordinary conformal assumptions are difficult to satisfy in autoregressive free-form generation and highlights exchangeability and output-structure challenges.
venue: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics

admission.reason: The survey is useful for terminology and for identifying conformal assumptions that fail in NLP, but the abstract does not itself validate a calibration, abstention or online-shift method. The admission gate is for studies that materially strengthen an evaluation capability, not general survey coverage.

title: Conformal Risk Control
abstract: Extends conformal prediction from set coverage to control of expected monotone loss functions. The framework includes extensions for distribution shift and demonstrates risk control on both computer-vision and natural-language-processing losses.

admission.reason: Conformal risk control is relevant transfer methodology and includes NLP losses and distribution-shift extensions, but the open gap specifically concerns continuing non-stationary free-form communication. The corpus status already states that structured-generation risk-control results are present; this abstract does not establish the missing continual adaptation setting.

title: Summarization of changes in dynamic text collections using Latent Dirichlet Allocation model
abstract: Studies summarization of significant changes in evolving document collections rather than summarization of a static snapshot. It evaluates methods on Wikipedia revision histories and explicitly models information changes occurring during specified temporal intervals.

admission.reason: The paper concerns generating summaries of changes in evolving collections, but the abstract describes a summarization method rather than an evaluation framework for omission, current-state correctness, evidence support or calibrated abstention. Temporal vocabulary matches F6, but the required evaluation capability is not demonstrated. Its identifier is also UNCHECKED, making it less attractive than the admitted temporal-evaluation candidates.

title: On optimum recognition error and reject tradeoff
abstract: Characterizes pattern-recognition performance through the joint error-reject tradeoff and derives an optimum rejection rule. The work provides foundational theory for evaluating selective systems by considering error and useful coverage together.

admission.reason: The error-reject tradeoff is foundational to F10, but the abstracted description is generic pattern-recognition theory with no NLP, free-form generation or non-stationary component. More directly applicable verified selective-prediction papers are available, so this unchecked record does not justify a reading slot in the current gap-focused round.

title: Verification of Forecasts Expressed in Terms of Probability

admission.reason: No abstract is supplied, so the admission gate cannot establish from the provided evidence whether this paper develops or empirically evaluates probability calibration or a proper scoring rule in a way that materially strengthens F9. Admission would require an abstract or equivalent bibliographic summary showing the exact calibration or scoring contribution and evaluation setting; the UNCHECKED identifier further favors verification before consuming a reading slot.
